content_voiceover: This slide shows how the locus control region, or LCR, physically loops to activate different globin genes across development, and it's the mechanistic basis for a major new therapy. In the fetal state, the LCR loops to contact the gamma-globin genes, producing HbF, while the repressors ZBTB7A and BCL11A are kept away from the gamma promoters. After birth, BCL11A — recruited together with ZBTB7A — binds the gamma-globin promoters and represses them, redirecting the LCR loop toward the delta and beta genes instead, which is the molecular switch from fetal to adult hemoglobin. The clinical payoff: BCL11A haploinsufficiency, or therapeutic disruption of its erythroid-specific enhancer, de-represses gamma-globin and reactivates HbF production in adults. This is exactly the mechanism behind the CRISPR gene therapy exagamglogene autotemcel, brand name Casgevy, which edits the BCL11A erythroid enhancer in a patient's own stem cells to raise fetal hemoglobin and treat sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia. Know that BCL11A is the master repressor of gamma-globin, and that its erythroid enhancer is now a validated gene therapy target.
keypoints: LCR loops to activate γ-globin (fetal) or β/δ-globin (adult)
BCL11A + ZBTB7A repress γ-globin postnatally → HbF to HbA switch
Target of CRISPR gene therapy (exa-cel/Casgevy) for SCD, β-thalassemia
keypoint_voiceover: Key points on fetal hemoglobin control. The locus control region loops to activate gamma-globin in the fetal state, and beta-globin in adults. BCL11A, working with ZBTB7A, represses gamma-globin after birth to drive the fetal-to-adult hemoglobin switch. BCL11A haploinsufficiency leads to persistent fetal hemoglobin. And this is the actual target of the approved CRISPR gene therapy, exa-cel or Casgevy, which edits the BCL11A erythroid enhancer to treat sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia.
